description.value: The study compared the diagnostic performance of ASL-based and FDG-PET-based Z-maps for visually distinguishing patients with neurodegenerative dementia from controls.

spans.text: The aim of this study was to compare ASL-based to FDG-PET-based Z-score maps in patients with neurodegenerative dementia, using visual assessment.

description.value: Data were collected from two separate sites in patients with Alzheimer’s disease or frontotemporal dementia and controls; ASL MRI and FDG-PET were acquired on separate occasions within 6 months, and readers assessed the resulting Z-maps blinded to modality and diagnosis.

spans.text: Data from two cohorts were collected from separate study sites, one in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, and one in Uppsala, Sweden.
The Z-maps of patients and controls from both modalities were presented randomly and blinded with regard to diagnosis and modality used to construct the image.

definition.value: Discrimination of patients versus controls using ASL-based Z-maps yielded high specificity (84%) and positive predictive value (80%), but significantly lower sensitivity compared to FDG-PET-based Z-maps (53% vs. 96%, p < 0.001).

spans.text: Acquisition time was approximately 4 min at both sites.
All subjects were scanned using a 3T MRI scanner with an 8-channel head coil
a pseudocontinuous ASL perfusion sequence

In Amsterdam, the ASL pulse-sequence employed a 3D FSE readout with background suppression; post-label delay = 2.0 s; TR = 9 ms; TE = 4.8 s; spiral readout with 8 arms × 512 samples; 36 × 5.0 mm axial slices; 3.2 × 3.2 mm  in-plane resolution; reconstructed pixel size = 1.7 × 1.7 mm . In Uppsala the ASL pulse-sequence used a 2D GRE readout with background suppression: TR = 4,100 ms, TE = 14 ms, FOV = 230 × 230 mm, pixel size = 2.75 × 2.75 mm, 30 dynamic scans, 20 slices of 5 mm, flip angle 90°.
The Amsterdam protocol included a 15-min scan
after injection of  F-FDG (FDG).

instructions.value: Readers were instructed through a tutorial using typical Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia cases, with an overview publication on deficit patterns, to familiarize them with the interface and promote a common assessment strategy. They classified each Z-map as healthy control or patient and, for pathological images, made a differential diagnosis between Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.

spans.text: The purpose was to familiarize the readers with the graphical appearance of the current interface and to promote a common assessment strategy.

stimuli.value: Thresholded ASL-perfusion-based and FDG-metabolism-based Z-score maps from 83 subjects, presented as dichromatic overlays on averaged heavily smoothed grayscale brain images in sagittal, transversal, and coronal views.
